"I'm going to post a reply to everyone," Gargi said, thumbs already typing. "I'll tell them exactly what I think."
"Wait," Harsha said, putting his hand over her phone. "If you post, they'll screenshot that too. It'll become bigger."
"So I just sit here?"
"No. Let me handle Vinit." Harsha opened his own chat. He typed: That isn't true. Please delete it.
"That's it?"
"That's it. No insults."
Harsha's mother came in with two plates of poha. She looked at Gargi's red eyes. "What happened, kanna?"
Gargi hesitated. Harsha nodded at her. "Tell her. And tomorrow we'll go to Rao sir together."
Gargi put her phone down and started talking.

qa.q: What message did Harsha send to Vinit?
qa.a: He typed: That isn't true. Please delete it.

qa.q: Why did Gargi want to post a reply to everyone?
qa.a: She was hurt and angry and wanted to defend herself by telling everyone exactly what she thought.

qa.q: Why does Harsha's way work better than a big public reply?
qa.a: A calm private request to the spreader does not give the rumour new fuel, and helping Gargi talk to his mother and Rao sir gets her real support.

qa.q: How might Harsha's mother feel when Gargi starts talking?
qa.a: She probably feels concerned but glad Gargi trusts her, and ready to help.

grounding: It shows a calm friend asking the spreader to delete a false story and steering the target toward a parent and teacher instead of a public denial.

I'm Akash. Last term, when that edited picture of Jahnavi went round, she wanted to make a video and "destroy them all." I understood. I was angry too. But I'd seen what happened to another girl who replied in public: fifty new comments by morning.
So I did two things. I messaged the three boys who first shared it, one by one: "It's not true. Please delete it." Two did. One laughed, but at least he stopped posting.
Then I sat with Jahnavi outside the staff room until she was ready to knock on Mrs Kulkarni's door. I didn't do the talking. I just stayed.
Looking back, the quiet stuff did more than any video could have.

qa.q: How many of the three boys deleted the picture?
qa.a: Two of the three boys deleted it.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when Jahnavi wanted to make a video?
qa.a: Akash understood and felt angry too, but was worried a public reply would bring more comments, like it had for another girl.

qa.q: Which of Akash's steps do you think helped Jahnavi most, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with her until she was ready to talk to Mrs Kulkarni, because it got her adult support without making the rumour bigger. 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Jahnavi to have Akash wait with her outside the staff room?
qa.a: She likely felt less alone and braver, knowing a friend was beside her while she spoke for herself.

grounding: It illustrates a friend calmly asking spreaders to delete a false picture and supporting the target to reach a teacher, instead of a public denial.

passage:
Teacher's note, Friday

This morning Tushar from 9A came to the staffroom with Ruchi. He had noticed a message going round the class chat claiming Ruchi had cheated in the unit test.

He told me he had already messaged the three students who posted it: "That is not true. Please delete it." Two of them did. He had not argued in the group itself.

Ruchi said she had wanted to post a long reply in the group, in capitals. Tushar had persuaded her not to, and said it would only make more people read it. Instead he walked her here.

Ruchi was shaky but calm. I thanked Tushar and told Ruchi she had done the right thing by coming to me. I checked her test paper with her, spoke to the third student before lunch, and called Ruchi's father so he would hear it from the school first.

— Vijay Sir

qa.q: What did Tushar message the three students who posted it?
qa.a: "That is not true. Please delete it."

qa.q: How did Ruchi feel when she wanted to post a long reply in capitals?
qa.a: She felt angry and upset, wanting to defend herself loudly in the group.

qa.q: Why was Tushar's approach better than a big public reply?
qa.a: A calm private request to delete, plus helping Ruchi reach a teacher, stopped the spread without making more people read the rumour.

qa.q: How might Ruchi's father feel hearing about it from the school first?
qa.a: He may feel reassured and less alarmed, knowing the school is handling it and Ruchi did nothing wrong.

grounding: A teacher's note shows Tushar calmly asking spreaders to delete a false rumour and helping Ruchi reach a teacher instead of replying publicly.

passage:
Tuesday night

Something happened today and I think I handled it okay.

Sumit forwarded a meme in the football group saying Rehan's family was kicked out of their flat for not paying rent. Rehan is in my class. He hasn't said anything, but he's been quiet all week.

I didn't reply in the group. I messaged Sumit privately: "That is not true, please delete it." He said, "How do you know?" I said, "Rehan's family moved because his dad got transferred. I helped them pack." He deleted it.

Then I went to Rehan at the bus stop. He said he wanted to post a video telling everyone to shut up. I told him that would only make more people see it. I said let's tell Coach instead. We went back in and told Coach together. Coach said he'd speak to the team at practice tomorrow and message Rehan's mum tonight.

Rehan said thanks. I think he meant it.

— Shankar

qa.q: Why did Rehan's family actually move?
qa.a: Because his dad got transferred.

qa.q: How did Rehan feel when he wanted to post a video telling everyone to shut up?
qa.a: He felt angry and hurt, wanting to hit back publicly at the rumour.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that helped without feeding the rumour?
qa.a: Shankar asked Sumit privately to delete it, avoided arguing in the group, and helped Rehan tell Coach the same day.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when Shankar said he helped them pack?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed and caught out, realising the meme was false.

grounding: Shankar calmly tells Sumit a rumour is untrue and to delete it, then helps Rehan tell a coach instead of replying publicly.

passage:
In Kalimpong, the school bus wound down the hill while Elizabeth stared at her phone, eyes wet. Someone in the Class 10 group had posted that she'd been sent home drunk from the Christmas programme. She had been sent home with a fever.
"I'm going to write a long message and tell everyone they're liars," Elizabeth said, thumbs shaking.
Dolma put a hand over the screen. "Wait. If you fight in the group, they'll screenshot that too."
Instead Dolma messaged the two boys who had shared it, separately: "That is not true. Please delete it." One did within minutes.
At the next stop, Dolma said, "Let's go to Lepcha Ma'am before assembly. I'll come with you." They went. Lepcha Ma'am listened, wrote down the names, and phoned Elizabeth's mother before first period.

qa.q: Why had Elizabeth actually been sent home from the Christmas programme?
qa.a: She had been sent home with a fever.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling as she planned a long message calling everyone liars?
qa.a: She felt angry and hurt, with wet eyes and shaking thumbs, desperate to defend herself in public.

qa.q: Why did Dolma's approach work better than a public reply?
qa.a: Dolma corrected it privately with the sharers and took Elizabeth to a teacher, which slowed the spread without giving the group a fresh fight to screenshot.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's mother feel when Lepcha Ma'am phones her?
qa.a: She would probably be upset about the rumour but relieved that the school is taking it seriously and that Elizabeth had support.

grounding: Shows a calm friend asking sharers to delete a false rumour and helping the target go to a teacher instead of replying publicly.
